paras: The lynching of Sills Spinks and Juster Jennings was the shooting of two Black men by a white posse near Grimes, Dale County, Alabama, late on the night of Thursday, July 29, 1920. The posse was hunting the assailant of a white woman, and the killings were followed by beatings, a lodge-hall burning and expulsions. A grand jury investigated and warrants were reported for three white men, but no outcome appears in the coverage.

Andrew Spinks, a Black man, was being held in the Montgomery county jail on a charge of attempted criminal assault on Mrs. Dassenger, the wife of a farmer near Grimes, close to the Dale-Houston county line. According to the Montgomery Advertiser, Sheriff Gamble had spirited him out of the county, first to the Pike county jail, after he "narrowly escaped lynching."

On Thursday evening Mrs. Dassenger, alone at home, was struck from behind with a heavy weapon; the wires alleged that Sills Spinks did it to keep her from testifying against his father. Her husband summoned a posse, and posses went out that night, rounding up the Black residents of the Dasinger place in an effort to identify the assailant. Spinks was captured and "his body riddled with bullets," and Jennings, said to be implicated, was shot after he reportedly seized a gun from one of his captors.

The two bodies lay in a public road until about 11 o'clock Friday morning. During the round-up two Black women were beaten, and on Friday night a Black man, Richard Jones, was shot, his arm and leg broken, while another man was severely whipped and ordered out of the county. A Black lodge hall near Grimes was burned that night, and Spinks' wife was given twenty-four hours to leave, departing, in the Associated Press's words, "after orders from white 'committees.'"

Coroner White investigated but disclosed nothing about any white residents' involvement, and Black residents were warned to stay in their homes. In mid-August Judge J. S. Williams charged the grand jury to go to the "bottom" of the lynching and to return indictments regardless of where they might fall. About 300 people from the Midland City and Grimes community testified, Mrs. Dassenger among them, and warrants for three white men said to be responsible for one of the deaths had not yet been served on August 18. No report of the grand jury's findings, or of any indictment or trial of white men, was found.

On August 26 Andrew Spinks pleaded guilty at Ozark and was sentenced to twenty years, before a crowd the Advertiser put at over 1,000 people from the Grimes and Midland City sections. The Chicago Whip's correspondent reported that "Fully 10,000 colored people deserted the county" after the lynchings and that circular letters urged Black residents to stay.

Alabama's white papers reported the killings as the consequence of a "murderous attack," and the Montgomery Advertiser described the lynchers as men who had "sought to mete out justice." Its August 18 report said Sills Spinks had sought to silence a witness and had "paid the full penalty for his action." Wire versions ran in Washington, South Carolina, Missouri, Mississippi and Tennessee under headlines such as "Alabama Mob Lynches Two Negroes" and "Posse Rounding Up Negroes Kills Two," all giving the posse's account.

The Chicago Whip called the posse "blood-thirsty cannibals," said the men were shot on their way to work, and reported that the inquest found no evidence connecting them to the crime. Under the headline "Flimsy Identity," the Chicago Defender and Phoenix Tribune said Mrs. Dassenger only "thought" her attacker was colored, judging by his foot, and that the men died without knowing the charge. The Richmond Planet, by contrast, reprinted the white wires almost unchanged, while Associated Negro Press briefs stressed the warnings to leave.

Accounts differ on how the men died: the Montgomery wire said Jennings seized a captor's gun, the Dothan wire attributed the gun-snatching to Spinks, and both versions came from the posse's side. Early dispatches dated the killings Thursday night, July 29, later reports July 30, and Associated Negro Press items "last Saturday night"; most placed them at Grimes, the Dothan wire at Midland City.

reader.title: Lynching of Sills Spinks and Juster Jennings
bases: Two Black men accused in an attack on a white woman were shot to death by a posse of white citizens, which the white and Black press alike called a lynching, and the killings were followed by beatings, a lodge-hall burning and expulsions (A1, A5, A13, A18).

Sills Spinks and Juster Jennings were shot to death by a citizens' posse, described as a mob, summoned by the woman's husband, with no lawful authority reported, after an alleged attack on a white woman (A5, A6, A1); a grand jury was charged to investigate the 'lynching' and warrants were issued for three white men (A17, A20).

The killings, names and place are reported independently by a Montgomery Advertiser special, AP and Dothan wires, and Black-press accounts (A1, A2, A6, A13), though the circumstances of the shootings are disputed (A5, A13, A29).

accounts.label: Posse's version (Montgomery and Dothan wires)
accounts.gist: Sills Spinks felled Mrs. Dassenger and said she would never testify against his father; the posse captured and shot him, and Jennings was shot after seizing a captor's gun (Montgomery wire) or Spinks was shot snatching a gun and Jennings killed later (Dothan wire).

accounts.label: Local white press
accounts.gist: The Advertiser described the lynchers as men seeking to 'mete out justice' and said the son 'paid the full penalty' for an attack meant to silence a witness.

accounts.label: Black correspondents (Defender, Whip)
accounts.gist: The men were seized on the street a block from the house, or met on their way to work the next morning, and shot without being allowed to speak; the woman only 'thought' her assailant was colored, and the inquest found no evidence against them.

framing.detail: The Montgomery Advertiser wrote of efforts to 'calm the passions of those who have sought to mete out justice' and said Sills Spinks 'paid the full penalty for his action'.
Wire headlines read 'Alabama Mob Lynches Two Negroes', 'Two Negroes Killed for Attacking Woman' and 'Posse Rounding Up Negroes Kills Two', each giving the posse's account.
Later AP items, 'Lynching Indictments Are Believed Probable' and 'May Indict Lynchers', still called the precipitating act 'Spinks' murderous attack'.

The Chicago Whip called the posse 'blood-thirsty cannibals' in 'lynchland' and said the men were innocent; the Defender and Phoenix Tribune ran 'Flimsy Identity' and 'Extra Large Feet Condemn Black Men in Old Alabama'.
The Richmond Planet printed the white wires' account of the 'alleged assailants' with little change.

versions.value: the morning after the women were beaten

conflicts.note: The earliest dispatches (Ozark and Dothan, July 30-31) put the killings on Thursday night; the July 30 date and the ANP 'Saturday' appear only in later reports.
The Advertiser later placed both communities in the same section of Dale County (A22); the Whip's 'outskirts of Montgomery' follows its Montgomery dateline.
